opus-5.5.text:
Honestly? I'd say we've made enormous progress on the small questions and very little on the big ones. And I say that as someone who's spent his career in this field, so it's not a complaint, it's just an honest assessment.

If you look at what neuroscience can do today, it's remarkable. I've worked with patients who have electrodes implanted directly in their brains, usually for clinical reasons like epilepsy, and we can record from individual neurons. We can see a cell that fires when you think about a specific person or a specific idea. We can sometimes predict what you're about to decide a second or more before you're aware you've decided it. A decade or two ago that would have sounded like science fiction.

But when you ask, "What is consciousness? Why does it feel like something to be me?" we're still largely where the philosophers were. We have better tools for finding correlates, meaning that when you're aware of something, this region lights up or this pattern shows up. Correlation isn't explanation, though. We don't have a theory that says, "Here's why this lump of tissue produces an experience." There are competing frameworks, integrated information theory, global workspace theory, and others, and there have been serious attempts to test them against each other. The results have mostly been humbling for everyone involved.

Free will is a similar story, with a twist. The experiments, going back to Libet and continuing with the work I and others have done, suggest that a lot of what we call decisions is set in motion before we're consciously aware of it. People hear that and conclude free will is dead. I think that's too fast. What the data really shows is that the conscious "I" is often more of a narrator than an author. It arrives a bit late and tells a story about why we did what we did. Whether there's still room for some kind of agency, maybe a veto, maybe the ability to shape the environment that shapes our future decisions, is still very much open.

The way I like to put it is that neuroscience is very good at telling you how the brain does things, and still quite bad at telling you who, if anyone, is doing them. What I find exciting is that these questions have moved from the armchair into the lab. We can actually run experiments now. We just have to be honest that the experiments so far have mostly shown us how strange the problem is, not how to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consciousness and free will as separate unresolved topics but does not suggest that they may be connected.

r002.rationale: It describes major progress on small questions and limited progress on big ones, but does not say that small advances on the major questions can make a meaningful difference.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly? I'd say we've made enormous progress on the small questions and almost none on the big ones, and I think that's worth being candid about.

If you'd asked a neuroscientist thirty years ago what we'd know by now, they'd have been impressed. We can record from thousands of neurons at once. I've sat in operating rooms with patients who have electrodes in their brains and watched a single cell fire when they think about a specific person. We can decode, roughly, what image someone is looking at, what word they're about to say. That's real. That's not hype.

But consciousness itself, the question of why any of that activity feels like something from the inside, we haven't moved the needle. We've gotten very good at describing the correlates. We can say "when you're aware of this, these regions light up, this oscillation happens." What we can't do is explain why those correlates produce experience rather than just processing. The hard problem is still hard. And I'd argue a lot of what gets published as "theories of consciousness" is really theories of attention, or theories of reportability, dressed up.

Free will is a little different, because there I think the science has actually told us something, it's just not what people wanted to hear. Experiments going back to Libet, and much better ones since, show that your brain commits to a decision before you're aware of deciding. I've seen it in my own work. We can predict, with some accuracy, which choice you'll make seconds before you report making it. So the folk picture, this little conscious pilot sitting in the cockpit pulling levers, that doesn't survive contact with the data.

But I'm careful here, because "free will doesn't exist" is a lazy headline. What the data really says is that the "you" doing the choosing is bigger than the part of you that narrates. The decision is still yours, it's just made by a system you don't have full introspective access to. Whether that counts as freedom is partly a philosophical question, and neuroscience shouldn't pretend to settle it.

So my honest scorecard: mechanisms, A-plus. Big questions, we've mostly learned to ask them better. And I'd rather admit that than oversell it, because the overselling is what makes people stop trusting us.

r001.rationale: The response links free will to conscious awareness: it says the brain commits to a decision before the person is aware of deciding, and describes the chooser as larger than the part that narrates.

r002.rationale: The response says neuroscience has made enormous progress on small questions and little progress on big ones, but does not say that small advances on the major unresolved questions can make a meaningful difference.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made enormous progress in measuring the brain, but we have to distinguish that from understanding it. We can ask much more precise questions now about perception, memory, and decision-making. But consciousness and free will are difficult partly because we don’t agree on exactly what we’re trying to explain.

With consciousness, are you asking how the brain distinguishes being awake from being asleep, or why any brain activity feels like something from the inside? Those are different questions. Making progress on the first doesn’t automatically solve the second.

And with free will, finding brain activity that precedes someone’s reported decision is interesting, but it doesn’t by itself establish that they have no freedom. It tells us that some of the process happens before they become aware of it. Whether that rules out free will depends on what you mean by free will.

So I’m optimistic about the science, but cautious about the big claims. We’re getting better at turning pieces of these questions into experiments. That’s real progress, even if it isn’t yet the final answer people want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consciousness and free will side by side, but does not suggest that they may be connected.

r002.rationale: It says that breaking the questions into experimental pieces and making progress on them is “real progress,” even without a final answer, conveying that incremental advances matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we've made enormous progress in understanding the machinery, and much less progress in agreeing on what would count as answering those questions. With consciousness, for example, we can study what changes when you fall asleep, undergo anesthesia, or become aware of an image. But explaining why any of that activity comes with a subjective experience is a different challenge.

Free will has a similar problem: what exactly are we testing? If you mean that your decisions have no prior causes, that's difficult to reconcile with studying the brain as a physical system. If you mean that you can deliberate, consider consequences, and change your behavior, those are real capacities we can investigate.

You often hear that neuroscience has disproved free will because brain activity can precede a person's reported awareness of deciding. I think that's too strong. Predicting something about a simple movement before someone reports deciding to move doesn't settle whether they freely chose a career or changed their mind in an argument.

So I'm optimistic about the experiments, but cautious about the big declarations. We're getting better at turning pieces of these questions into things we can measure. That doesn't mean we've solved the whole question.
